newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Heavy fighting north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting north of Kabul.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban launched an offensive against forces of the ousted government and their allies on Saturday night.
"We launched a big offensive at 9 p.m. (1630 GMT) last night," said Taleban commander Mullah Rakhmatullah on Sunday morning. "We have recaptured Gul Dara village and are continuing our advance."
It was impossible to independently verify his comments.
The attack was launched along the so-called old road which runs up the western side of the broad valley that runs north from Kabul.
For the last month the front line has remained static, despite numerous attempts by the opposition to push back the Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27.
Throughout Saturday night and Sunday morning, the sound of rocket and artillery fire was clearly audible in Kabul itself, some 20 km (13 miles) from the scene of the fighting.
Both sides were still exchanging heavy barrages of artillery and rockets on Sunday morning.

Taleban multi-barrelled rocket launchers were firing salvo after salvo of rockets towards the positions of the alliance forces while behind the front lines, tank crews were cleaning shells in preparation for going up to the lines.
A steady trickle of families -- their possessions loaded on to donkeys and wheelbarrows -- moved south.
A shepherd who was also moving south with his livestock told Reuters: "This is the heaviest fighting I have seen since the Taleban were forced back (in mid-October)."

The Taleban are fighting an alliance comprised of the forces of the ousted government under Ahmed Shah Masood and their allies under General Abdul Rashid Dostum on two fronts, one just north of Kabul and another in the remote northwestern provinces of Badghis and Faryab.
On the Kabul front, the Taleban hold a strategic line of low hills that the alliance must capture if they are to launch an offensive against Kabul itself.
The Taleban have vowed to disarm other armed groups in Afghanistan and impose their puritanical vision of Islam on the whole country.
The Taleban have agreed in principle to the necessity of a ceasefire, but their demands are unlikely to be acceptable to their opposition.
The two sides met under the auspices of the United Nations in the Pakistani Islamabad on November 7 for what the U.N. decribed as technical level discussions about a ceasefire.
Although the negotiations were said to be amicable, the two sides failed to come to an agreement.
